subject: physics
title: Gap Jump
summary: Lift an electron across the band gap of Ge, Si and carbon, then dope a silicon crystal and count its electrons and holes.

chapter.name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits

ncertRef: Section 14.2, Classification of metals, conductors and semiconductors
concepts: Energy bands and the band gap
learningOutcome: The student can find the longest wavelength that lifts an electron across a band gap with hc/E_g, and the electron and hole counts of a doped crystal from the dopant and n_e n_h = n_i².

levels.title: Sparky’s jump
levels.adds: Baseline: an electron crosses the gap only if the photon carries at least E_g, so the longest useful wavelength is hc/E_g (Ex 14.3; Example 14.1).
hints: Germanium 0.7 eV, silicon 1.1 eV, carbon 5.4 eV.
The photon energy is hc/λ with hc = 1240 eV nm.
A bigger gap needs a shorter wavelength.

levels.title: Doper’s crystal
levels.adds: New idea: each dopant atom adds one carrier, which sets the majority count; the minority count follows from n_e n_h = n_i² (Ex 14.1, 14.2; Example 14.2).
hints: 1 ppm means one atom in a million: multiply the 5 × 10²⁸ atoms by 10⁻⁶.
5 valence electrons make electrons the majority; 3 make holes the majority.
The scarce carrier is n_i² divided by the common one; with powers of ten, the two exponents add up to 2 × log n_i.

misconceptions: A semiconductor has no band gap
A p-type crystal is positively charged
Doping creates more carriers of both kinds
